title: Walaeus: justifying fiducia is a will-act receiving Christ — not intellect’s remitted-assent
source_text: LIII. Et eodem etiam redire videntur quae docet Antonius Walaeus in locis communibus, titulo De nostri Justificatione coram Deo. Postquam enim sibi proposuit illam objectionem, qua videtur probari fidem non esse fiduciam: Si fides est fiducia remissionis peccatorum, tum per fidem non possemus justificari, quia justificatio est effectus fidei: effectum autem fidei non potest esse ejus primum objectum, cum omne objectum actum potentiae, a qua apprehenditur, antecedat. Respondet, negando Actum primum fidei quo justificamur, esse actum illum quo creditur remissio peccatorum, sed quo recipitur Christus cum merito ejus in remissionem peccatorum, non praeteritam, sed sequentem; Atque istud non tam per assensum particularem, quam per fiduciam illam voluntatis a generali assensu sequitur. Non possumus enim, inquit, assentiri rei nisi verae. Atqui quum nondum apprehendimus Christum per fidem, nondum est verum nobis esse remissa peccata, sed si verum ipsum credimus. Unde patet juxta Walaeum fiduciam qua justificamur esse actum voluntatis, non intellectus, eamque nasci ex assensu generali quem promissionibus Evangelii adhibemus, & praecedere assensum specialem quo certi sumus de remissione peccatorum nostrorum, quae proprium & directum ejus objectum non est, sed Christus cum merito ejus. Quae plane consonant cum supra exposita Amesii sententia.
pass_a_gloss: And to the same also seem to come what Anthony Walaeus teaches in the Common Places, under the title On our Justification before God. For after he set before himself that objection by which faith seems proved not to be trust: If faith is trust of the remission of sins, then we could not be justified by faith, because justification is an effect of faith: but an effect of faith cannot be its first object, since every object precedes the act of the power by which it is apprehended. He answers by denying that the first act of faith by which we are justified is that act by which remission of sins is believed, but that by which Christ with His merit is received unto remission of sins — not past, but following; And that this follows not so much by particular assent as by that trust of the will from general assent. For we cannot, he says, assent to a thing unless it is true. But when we have not yet apprehended Christ by faith, it is not yet true that sins have been remitted to us, but if we believe the thing itself as true. Whence it is plain according to Walaeus that the trust by which we are justified is an act of the will, not of the intellect, and that it is born from the general assent which we give to the promises of the Gospel, and precedes the special assent by which we are sure of the remission of our sins — which is not its proper and direct object, but Christ with His merit. Which plainly agree with Ames's opinion set forth above.
pass_b_english: Walaeus faces the objection: if faith = trust of remitted sins, justification can’t be faith’s effect.
Answer: first justifying act is receiving Christ with His merit unto coming remission — not believing sins already remitted.
Will’s fiducia from general Gospel assent — precedes special remitted-assent.
Proper object = Christ and His merit, not the remitted-proposition.
